title: Quadratics Part 1
lead: Quadratics are the heart of the Advanced Math domain. This class covers the foundation: what a quadratic is, its three forms, factoring, multiplying and simplifying expressions, and how a quadratic looks on a graph. Class 11 builds on it with the quadratic formula, completing the square and the discriminant.

parts.title: Part 1 · The core idea
parts.html:
A quadratic is any expression with x² as its highest power: ax² + bx + c, where a is not zero. Every quadratic graphs as a parabola, a smooth U-shaped curve. If a > 0 it opens upward and has a minimum. If a < 0 it opens downward and has a maximum.

The three most important points on a parabola:

  • Roots (zeros, x-intercepts): where the parabola crosses the x-axis, where y = 0. These are the solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0.
  • The vertex: the turning point, a minimum if it opens up and a maximum if it opens down.
  • The y-intercept: where it crosses the y-axis, always at (0, c) in standard form.

parts.title: Part 2 · The three forms
parts.html:
Each form of a quadratic reveals different information at a glance.

FormLooks likeShows at once
Standardax² + bx + cThe y-intercept, c
Factoreda(x − r₁)(x − r₂)The roots, r₁ and r₂
Vertexa(x − h)² + kThe vertex, (h, k)

Factored form shows the roots because the product is zero when either factor is zero. y = (x − 3)(x + 5) has roots x = 3 and x = −5. Watch the signs: (x + 5) gives the root −5, not +5.

Vertex form has the same sign trap. y = (x − 2)² + 7 has vertex (2, 7). y = 3(x + 4)² − 1 has vertex (−4, −1), because x + 4 = x − (−4).

Many questions are conversions in disguise. Expanding takes factored or vertex form to standard form. Factoring takes standard form to the roots. Completing the square (Class 11) takes standard form to the vertex.

Tip. Read the question first to know which form to reach for. Roots asked → factored form. Vertex, minimum or maximum asked → vertex form. y-intercept asked → the c in standard form. If the given form does not show what is asked, the question wants you to convert or factor.

parts.title: Part 3 · Factoring and solving
parts.html:
Factoring is the fastest way to solve a quadratic when the numbers are friendly. It rests on the zero product property: if two things multiply to zero, one of them is zero.

  1. Move everything to one side so the other side is 0.
  2. Factor the expression.
  3. Set each factor equal to 0 and solve.

When the x² coefficient is 1: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.

x2+7x+12=0 Multiply to 12, add to 7 → 3 and 4 → (x+3)(x+4)=0 → x=−3 or x=−4
x2−x−12=0 Multiply to −12, add to −1 → −4 and +3 → (x−4)(x+3)=0 → x=4 or x=−3

When the x² coefficient is not 1: multiply a and c, find two numbers that multiply to that product and add to b, split the middle term with them, and factor in pairs.

3x2+10x+8=0 a·c=24; multiply to 24, add to 10 → 6 and 4
Split the middle term → 3x2+6x+4x+8=0
Factor in pairs → 3x(x+2)+4(x+2)=0
(3x+4)(x+2)=0 → x=−43 or x=−2

Patterns to know on sight.

PatternRuleExample
Difference of squaresa² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)4x² − 49 = (2x − 7)(2x + 7)
Perfect square, plusa² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²x² + 10x + 25 = (x + 5)²
Perfect square, minusa² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)²x² − 6x + 9 = (x − 3)²

Take out a common factor first. It makes everything after it simpler.

5x2−20x=0 Factor out 5x → 5x(x−4)=0 → x=0 or x=4

Common mistakes. Dividing both sides by x throws away the solution x = 0. Factoring without first making one side 0 gives factors you cannot use. And the factor (x + 3) gives the solution −3, not 3.

Not every quadratic factors with whole numbers. When it does not, use the quadratic formula or complete the square, both in Class 11.

parts.title: Part 4 · Polynomial operations and rational expressions
parts.html:
These are the “which expression is equivalent to…?” questions. They use factoring in reverse and forwards.

Multiplying polynomials. Use the distributive property: every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second.

(2x+3)(x−5) 2x2−10x+3x−15=2x2−7x−15

Adding algebraic fractions. You must find a common denominator first. In general, A/x + B/y = (Ay + Bx) / xy.

2x+3x+1 Common denominator: x(x+1)
2(x+1)+3xx(x+1)=5x+2x(x+1)

Simplifying. Factor the numerator and the denominator first, then cancel common factors.

x2−9x+3 (x+3)(x−3)x+3=x−3

Common mistake. Cancelling terms that are added, not multiplied. In (x² − 9) / (x + 3) you cannot cancel the x's or divide 9 by 3. Only whole factors cancel, which is why you factor first.

Rational equations. If P(x) / Q(x) = 0, then P(x) = 0. Always check that your solution does not make the denominator Q(x) zero. Class 21 works through these in full.

Desmos check. For an equivalence question, graph the original expression and each choice. The equivalent one draws exactly the same curve.

parts.title: Part 5 · Reading a quadratic graph or table
parts.html:
• Roots visible on the x-axis? They are the numbers in factored form. Roots 2 and 5 mean y = a(x − 2)(x − 5) for some a.
  • Vertex visible? Use vertex form: y = a(x − h)² + k.
  • Axis of symmetry: the vertical line through the vertex. The vertex sits exactly midway between two points of equal height. If f(2) = f(10), the axis is x = 6. If you also know b, you can find a from x = −b/2a.

The midpoint rule works with roots too. If a quadratic has roots 3 and −9, the vertex's x-coordinate is (3 + (−9)) / 2 = −3.

Tables. Each point in a table is one equation, so each point lets you find one unknown coefficient. Three points determine the whole quadratic. Desmos regression handles these cleanly.

parts.title: Part 6 · The Desmos workflow
parts.html:
• Find roots: type the equation and click where the curve crosses the x-axis. This is a quick check on your factoring, and a way to answer “what are the solutions” when the numbers are awkward.
  • Find the vertex, maximum or minimum: type the function and click the turning point, which Desmos marks. Read the x-coordinate for “at what value of x” and the y-coordinate for the maximum or minimum value.
  • Solve ax² + bx + c = d: type the quadratic and the horizontal line y = d. The x-coordinates of the intersections are the solutions.
  • Unknown coefficient with a given point or root: define the function with a slider for the unknown, plot the given point and adjust. Then verify by substituting the value exactly.

When the question is conceptual (“which form shows the maximum”, “which is equivalent”), reasoning by hand is faster. Use Desmos when numbers or coordinates are asked for.

parts.title: Part 7 · Matching coefficients, and substituting a block
parts.html:
Matching coefficients. If two expressions are equivalent, they are equal for every value of x, so the coefficients of matching terms must be equal. Expand, line the terms up, and set them equal one pair at a time.

(x + 4)(x + b) and x² + 3bx + c are equivalent, where b and c are constants. What is the value of c? Expand the left side → x2+(b+4)x+4b
x terms: b+4=3b → b=2
Constants: c=4b=8

The same idea answers “the equation is true for all values of x” and “the equation has infinitely many solutions”: both sides must match term by term.

Substituting a block. When the same expression appears more than once, give it a single letter, solve, then put the expression back.

What is the positive solution of (x − 2)² − 3(x − 2) − 10 = 0? Let A=x−2 → A2−3A−10=0
Factor → (A−5)(A+2)=0 → A=5 or A=−2
Put x−2 back → x=7 or x=0
Positive solution: 7

The same works for factoring: in x²(x − 3) − 4(x − 3), the block (x − 3) is a common factor, giving (x − 3)(x² − 4) = (x − 3)(x − 2)(x + 2).
